x.ASV: A Song; a Psalm of the sons of Korah. Great is Jehovah, and greatly to be praised, In the city of our God, in his holy mountain.
x.Darby: A Song; a Psalm. Of the sons of Korah. Great is Jehovah, and greatly to be praised in the city of ourGod, in the hill of his holiness.
x.KJV: A Song and Psalm for the sons of Korah. Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in the mountain of his holiness.
x.YLT: A Song, a Psalm, by sons of Korah. Great is Jehovah, and praised greatly, In the city of our God--His holy hill.

nt: The expression **is being praised** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people are praising him]

In this context, the verbal form has the implied sense that Yahweh “is to be praised” or “ought to be praised.” Your language may have a verbal form that indicates that explicitly. If so, it would be appropriate to use it here in your translation. If not, you may be able to indicate this sense in another way. Alternate translation: [and he is worthy to be praised]

Since the psalmist has used the name **Yahweh** earlier in this sentence, and since Yahweh is the same person as **our God**, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [in his city]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain**, Mount Zion, that is characterized by **holiness**. The idea is that Yahweh set apart this mountain as a place where he would be present in a special way and where people would worship him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the mountain that he set apart for himself] or [on the mountain that he made a sacred place]

x.ASV: Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, Is mount Zion, on the sides of the north, The city of the great King.
x.Darby: Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion, [on] the sides of the north, the city of the great King.
x.KJV: Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King.
x.YLT: Beautiful for elevation, A joy of all the land, is Mount Zion, The sides of the north, the city of a great king.

nt: Here the **earth** represents the people of the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the joy of all of the people of the earth]

The psalmist is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the joy of people from throughout the earth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something that makes people from throughout the earth rejoice]

This could mean: (1) that the psalmist is saying where on Mount Zion the **city** of Jerusalem, and especially the temple and the royal palace, are located. Alternate translation: [on its northern slope, where the city of the great king is] or (2) that the psalmist is using the phrase **the recesses of the north** in the same way as in [Isaiah 14:13](../isa/14/13.md) to mean the distant north, where pagan nations believe the council of the gods met. The psalmist would be saying that Yahweh is the supreme God who actually rules the council of supernatural beings (as in [89:7](../089/007.md)) from his temple in Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [, the site of Jerusalem, the place from which Yahweh, the great king, rules as the supreme God]

x.ASV: God hath made himself known in her palaces for a refuge.
x.Darby: God is known in her palaces as a high fortress.
x.KJV: God is known in her palaces for a refuge.
x.YLT: God in her high places is known for a tower.

nt: The expression **is known** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People know him as a stronghold] or [He has made himself known as a stronghold]
See how you translated the term “stronghold” in [46:7](../046/007.md) and [46:11](../046/011.md). Alternate translation: [as a protector]

x.ASV: For, lo, the kings assembled themselves, They passed by together.
x.Darby: For behold, the kings assembled themselves, they passed by together;
x.KJV: For, lo, the kings were assembled, they passed by together.
x.YLT: For, lo, the kings met, they passed by together,

nt: As is characteristic in a psalm of praise, the word **For** introduces the reason why people should praise Yahweh as the psalmist has been saying they should. Alternate translation: [We should praise Yahweh because]

The psalmist is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [listen]

x.ASV: They saw it, then were they amazed; They were dismayed, they hasted away.
x.Darby: They saw, — so they marvelled; they were troubled, they fled in consternation:
x.KJV: They saw it, and so they marvelled; they were troubled, and hasted away.
x.YLT: They have seen--so they have marvelled, They have been troubled, they were hastened away.

nt: The psalmist is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they saw** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this action took place at the same time as when the kings **marveled**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [As soon as they saw it, they marveled]

The expression **were terrified** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [This terrified them]

In this clause, the psalmist is describing the result of the previous clause. It may be helpful to add a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [so they hastened themselves away]

x.ASV: Trembling took hold of them there, Pain, as of a woman in travail.
x.Darby: Trembling took hold upon them there; anguish, as of a woman in travail.
x.KJV: Fear took hold upon them there, and pain, as of a woman in travail.
x.YLT: Trembling hath seized them there, Pain, as of a travailing woman.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of **Trembling** as if it were a living thing that could have **seized** the enemy kings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There they trembled uncontrollably]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [pain seized them there, like that of childbearing]

The point of this comparison is not that these kings felt physical **pain** but that they cried out in anguish and distress as a woman would who was feeling the actual **pain** of **childbearing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they cried out uncontrollably in anguish and distress]

x.ASV: With the east wind Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish.
x.Darby: With an east wind thou hast broken the ships of Tarshish.
x.KJV: Thou breakest the ships of Tarshish with an east wind.
x.YLT: By an east wind Thou shiverest ships of Tarshish.

nt: The word **you** is singular here and through verse 11 because the psalmist is directly addressing Yahweh. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [you, Yahweh, shatter]

The psalmist is using **ships of Tarshish** as a common expression of his culture to mean “ocean-going ships” or “large, sturdy ships.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in [1 Kings 10:22](../1ki/10/22.md). Alternate translation: [ocean-going ships] or [large, sturdy ships]

x.ASV: As we have heard, so have we seen In the city of Jehovah of hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish it for ever. [Selah
x.Darby: As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of Jehovah of hosts, in the city of ourGod:God doth establish it for ever. Selah.
x.KJV: As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God: God will establish it for ever. Selah.
x.YLT: As we have heard, so we have seen, In the city of Jehovah of hosts, In the city of our God, God doth establish her--to the age. Selah.

nt: See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.

x.ASV: We have thought on thy lovingkindness, O God, In the midst of thy temple.
x.Darby: We have thought, OGod, of thy loving-kindness, in the midst of thy temple.
x.KJV: We have thought of thy lovingkindness, O God, in the midst of thy temple.
x.YLT: We have thought, O God, of Thy kindness, In the midst of Thy temple,

nt: The psalmist means that he and his fellow Judeans have **compared** the **covenant faithfulness** that God showed on this occasion with the past covenant faithfulness that their ancestors related to them, as described in the previous verse. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [We have compared your present covenant faithfulness with your past covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [We have compared how faithful you were to your covenant on this occasion with how faithful you were to your covenant in the past]

By **We**, The psalmist means himself and his fellow Judeans but not Yahweh, to whom he is speaking. So use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

x.ASV: As is thy name, O God, So is thy praise unto the ends of the earth: Thy right hand is full of righteousness.
x.Darby: According to thy name, OGod, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth: thy right hand is full of righteousness.
x.KJV: According to thy name, O God, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth: thy right hand is full of righteousness.
x.YLT: As is Thy name, O God, so is Thy praise, Over the ends of the earth, Righteousness hath filled Thy right hand.

nt: In this context, God’s **name** represents his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People to the ends of the earth praise you, God, as your reputation deserves]

The psalmist is speaking of **righteousness** as if it were an object with which God’s **right hand** could be **full**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your right hand is thoroughly characterized by righteousness]

Here, God’s **hand** represents his powerful activity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You powerfully bring about righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You powerfully do what is right]

x.ASV: Let mount Zion be glad, Let the daughters of Judah rejoice, Because of thy judgments.
x.Darby: Let mount Zion rejoice, let the daughters of Judah be glad, because of thy judgments.
x.KJV: Let mount Zion rejoice, let the daughters of Judah be glad, because of thy judgments.
x.YLT: Rejoice doth Mount Zion, The daughters of Judah are joyful, For the sake of Thy judgments.

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let Mount Zion and the daughters of Judah rejoice greatly] or [Let Mount Zion rejoice; yes, let the daughters of Judah be glad]

Here, **Mount Zion** represents the people who live on Mount Zion, that is, the people of the city of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let the people of Jerusalem rejoice]

This could mean: (1) that the psalmist is speaking of the kingdom of **Judah** were a mother and of its people as if they were her **daughters**. Alternate translation: [let the people of Judah be glad] or (2) that the psalmist is speaking specifically of the women of the kingdom of **Judah** and encouraging them to have a victory celebration, as women in this culture did. Alternate translation: [let the women of Judah hold a victory celebration]

x.ASV: Walk about Zion, and go round about her; Number the towers thereof;
x.Darby: Walk about Zion, and go round about her: count the towers thereof;
x.KJV: Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof.
x.YLT: Compass Zion, and go round her, count her towers,

nt: The instances of the implied “you” in the imperatives **Circle**, **go around**, and **Count** are plural because the psalmist is addressing many people. In the next verse, the terms “your” and “you” and the instances of the implied “you” in the imperatives are plural for the same reason. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Go all the way around Zion]

Since a mountain does not have **towers**, here **Zion** represents the city of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Circle the city on Mount Zion] or [Circle Jerusalem]

x.ASV: Mark ye well her bulwarks; Consider her palaces: That ye may tell it to the generation following.
x.Darby: Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces: that ye may tell it to the generation following.
x.KJV: Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following.
x.YLT: Set your heart to her bulwark, Consider her high places, So that ye recount to a later generation,

nt: The psalmist is using **put your heart to** as a common expression of his culture to mean “carefully consider.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [keep in mind her rampart] or [carefully consider her rampart]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **rampart**. He means all the ramparts of the walls of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [her ramparts]

x.ASV: For this God is our God for ever and ever: He will be our guide even unto death.
x.Darby: For thisGod is ourGod for ever and ever; he will be our guide until death.
x.KJV: For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death.
x.YLT: That this God is our God--To the age and for ever, He--he doth lead us over death!

nt: As in verse 4, here the word **For** introduces the reason why people should praise Yahweh. It is not introducing the reason why people should walk around the walls of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [We should praise this God because he is our God]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **He** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will guide us** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role of Yahweh in guiding the Judeans. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [He is the one who will guide us]
